prompt: A logistics company that runs an Apache Kafka cluster on premises (6 brokers, 2 TB of inflow per day) will migrate to AWS within two months. More than 50 producer and consumer applications that use 120 topics must continue to use the Kafka client library and the existing topic configuration as they are. The operations team has only two people and wants to reduce broker patching and failure recovery operations. The migration period is short, so rewriting applications is not in the schedule. After the migration, consumer group offset management and the topic retention period (7 days) must behave the same way. About 14 TB of broker storage capacity is required, and distribution across 3 Availability Zones is assumed. What should the company choose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Switch to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and rewrite the producers and consumers with the Kinesis SDK.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an Amazon MSK cluster and change only the bootstrap server addresses of the clients.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Install Kafka directly on 6 EC2 instances and operate ZooKeeper as well.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switch to Amazon SQS FIFO queues, map topics to queues, and modify the applications.

explanation: Amazon MSK is a managed service that supports the Kafka protocol and clients as they are, so only the connection address needs to change, and AWS handles broker patching and failure recovery. Kinesis Data Streams is not compatible with the Kafka API, so the clients would have to be rewritten. Installing directly on EC2 means continuing to operate patching and recovery, which conflicts with the requirement to reduce operational burden. SQS has a different model of topics, partitions, and consumer groups, so the application structure would have to change. The two-month schedule and the condition that rewriting is not possible require Kafka compatibility, and the staff of two requires a managed offering.

prompt: A medical imaging company replicates de-identified image files from an Amazon S3 bucket in us-east-1 to a bucket in eu-west-1 for use by its European analytics team, with about 4 TB uploaded per day. Versioning is turned on for both buckets. Under the internal SLA, most newly uploaded objects must be replicated within 15 minutes, and the operations team must receive a notification if replication is delayed. The operations team has two people, so custom-built copy logic is hard to maintain. Only objects under the raw/ prefix are to be replicated, and nothing else is replicated. The replication latency metric must be viewable in Amazon CloudWatch. Which method meets these requirements with the LEAST operational burden?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run same-Region replication and S3 Batch Operations every 15 minutes with an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Configure only default cross-Region replication and leave the replication completion time to the default behavior of the service.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn on S3 Replication Time Control for cross-Region replication and receive delay notifications.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Have an AWS Lambda function copy objects directly to the destination bucket on upload, and retry through Amazon SQS if the copy fails.

explanation: S3 Replication Time Control has an SLA of replicating most objects within seconds and 99.9% of them within 15 minutes, and it provides replication metrics and delay events, so the 15-minute target and the notification requirement are met with a managed feature. Same-Region replication does not match the requirement that the destination be in a different Region, and scheduled batches have no 15-minute guarantee. Default cross-Region replication can have replication metrics turned on separately, but it has no SLA for the 15-minute replication time and no events when a threshold is exceeded. A Lambda copy requires you to operate handling of large objects, retries, and ordering yourself, which is a large operational burden. Both an SLA figure and delay notifications are required, so the default configuration without a replication time guarantee is eliminated.

prompt: The event server of a mobile game (an average of 40 instances, up to 80 during surges) is operated in an Auto Scaling group. After an instance starts, it takes about 7 minutes to install the application and complete its configuration, so when connections suddenly surge, users get errors before new instances are put into service. An instance that has finished initialization can be put into service within tens of seconds even if it is stopped and started again. The timing of surges cannot be predicted, and keeping a large capacity running all the time is a cost burden. Traffic surges occur within 2 to 3 minutes right after an event notification is pushed, and the additional capacity needed in that period is about 40 instances. The target tracking policy is currently set with a target of 80% CPU utilization. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Keep initialized instances waiting in a stopped state in a warm pool and put them into service first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Raise the minimum capacity to the peak level and keep the instances running all the time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use scheduled scaling to increase capacity every evening and reduce it at dawn.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lower the CPU target of the target tracking policy from 80% to 30% so that it scales out earlier.

explanation: A warm pool keeps instances that have finished installation and configuration waiting in a stopped state and puts them into service first when scaling out, so the 7-minute initialization period is skipped. While stopped, there is no charge for the instance itself and only EBS volume and Elastic IP address charges apply, so it is cheaper than running instances all the time. Raising the minimum capacity to the peak solves the timing of the surge but always incurs a large cost. Scheduled scaling is effective only when the timing can be predicted and does not suit unpredictable surges. Lowering the CPU target increases instances even in normal times, raising costs, and the 7-minute delay after launch remains. The two constraints of unpredictable surges and the cost burden of always-on capacity point to pre-initialized stopped instances.

prompt: An Amazon ECS application of a SaaS company stores the Amazon RDS for MySQL password in a configuration file. A security audit pointed out that the password must be rotated every 90 days, and the application must read the new value without being redeployed when it is rotated. The four developers want to minimize self-built rotation scripts and their maintenance. Secret value retrieval is on the order of dozens of requests per second. The service must not be interrupted while the password changes, and the rotation history must remain as audit evidence. The databases are three RDS instances in the Asia Pacific (Seoul) Region, all in the same VPC. Which method meets these requirements with the LEAST operational burden?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Store it in a Parameter Store SecureString, run a self-written Lambda function on an EventBridge schedule to change the password, and update the parameter.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Encrypt the configuration file with AWS KMS and place it in Amazon S3, and turn on automatic KMS key rotation so that the database password changes periodically.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Have the instance user data script generate a new password every time it boots, apply it to RDS, and inject it as an environment variable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager, turn on automatic rotation for RDS, and have the application retrieve the secret value through the API at runtime.

explanation: The correct answer is automatic rotation for RDS in Secrets Manager. The managed rotation feature handles changing the database password and updating the secret value on a schedule, and the application receives the latest value each time it retrieves it, so no redeployment is needed; dozens of retrievals per second are well within the retrieval quota of 10,000 requests per second per Region. Parameter Store has no built-in rotation feature, so you would have to build and maintain a Lambda function. Automatic KMS key rotation only changes the encryption key material and has no effect on the database password. A boot-time script changes the password only at reboot time, and it gets out of sync with running instances. The condition to minimize self-built rotation scripts points to a service with a managed rotation feature.

prompt: The Amazon S3 bucket of a company that operates a document archiving service has versioning turned on, but its monthly storage cost keeps rising. Analysis shows that most of it is previous versions accumulated by tens of thousands of overwrites every day, plus a considerable amount of fragments from incomplete multipart uploads. After 30 days, no one requests recovery of previous versions, and incomplete uploads older than 7 days are never resumed. Current-version objects must be kept as they are. The bucket has about 8 million objects, and the company wants to solve the problem with only the console and lifecycle settings. The bucket is used by a document upload service, and the average file size is 80 MB, so multipart uploads are used. The current versions are read every day by the analytics team and therefore must not be touched. Which TWO actions reduce storage costs? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after a specified number of days.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Suspend versioning on the bucket so that existing previous versions are deleted automatically.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Switch to a Requester Pays bucket to shift the storage costs to the account that reads the data.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add a lifecycle rule that expires all objects 30 days after creation to clean up old data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Add a lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads after a specified number of days.

explanation: The correct answers are a rule that expires noncurrent versions and a rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads. Previous versions keep accumulating and incurring storage charges while versioning is on, so clean them up with a noncurrent version expiration rule, and because incomplete fragments are billed separately, remove them with an abort rule. Expiring all objects would delete current versions as well, which conflicts with the condition that they must be kept. Suspending versioning does not delete previous versions that have already accumulated. Requester Pays shifts only request and transfer charges, and the bucket owner continues to pay for storage. Because current versions must be kept, a rule that expires entire objects is eliminated, and rules that address each of the two cost causes, previous versions and incomplete fragments, are needed.

prompt: The editing room of a media company uploads original video files of 5 GB to 50 GB to an Amazon S3 bucket in the Asia Pacific (Seoul) Region over AWS Direct Connect and downloads them on Amazon EC2 instances used for rendering. Currently, the transfers use a single stream, so the bandwidth is not fully utilized, and if a transfer fails partway through, it is retried from the beginning. Network bandwidth is sufficient, and about 200 files are processed per day. Downloaded videos are used for rendering immediately, so there must be no restore wait. The upload client uses the AWS SDK, so the part size and the number of concurrent transfers can be specified in configuration. Rendering nodes sometimes start processing after reading only part of a video first. Which TWO actions should the company apply to increase throughput and reduce the cost of retries? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use multipart upload for uploads and transfer the parts in parallel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Store the objects in the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Send byte-range GET requests in parallel for downloads.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable bucket versioning so that a failed upload can be rolled back to the previous version.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Replicate the data to a bucket in a second Region to share the download load.

explanation: Multipart upload splits an object into parts and sends them in parallel to increase throughput, and only the failed parts need to be sent again; requesting byte-range GETs in parallel lets downloads also use the bandwidth over multiple connections and retry only part of the object. Glacier Flexible Retrieval is a low-cost archive class that requires a restore wait, so it would actually reduce immediate download performance. Versioning is a feature for recovering from overwrites and has nothing to do with upload throughput. Replicating to another Region only increases storage costs and does not solve the single-stream problem. Uploading and downloading are separate bottlenecks, so one parallelization technique is needed for each direction.

prompt: 200 Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets reach external destinations through a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, and the security policy requires allowing HTTPS outbound traffic only to 5 approved domains. The IP addresses of the domains change frequently, and attempts to connect directly by IP address must also be blocked. The instances are spread across 3 Availability Zones and availability cannot be reduced, and the security team does not want to update rules each time the IP addresses change. The allowed domains include a payment processor API and a package repository, and most of them are behind a CDN, so their IP addresses change often. Blocked requests must be logged so that the security team can review them once a month. Which method meets these requirements MOST appropriately?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall to block DNS queries for domains other than the approved ones so that instances cannot connect to other domains.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Register the approved domain names in the security group outbound rules and deny other destinations to control HTTPS traffic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Put the IP ranges of the approved domains in an allow list in the network ACL and update the rules with AWS Lambda whenever the IP addresses change.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a domain allow list rule group in AWS Network Firewall, leave all other traffic blocked by default, and place it in the outbound path.

explanation: The correct answer is the domain allow list in Network Firewall. It identifies the domain from information such as the SNI of the HTTPS connection and blocks traffic not on the list by default, so rules do not need to be changed when IP addresses change, and direct connections by IP address are also blocked. DNS Firewall filters only DNS queries, so connecting directly by IP address bypasses it. Security groups cannot specify domain names as rule targets. Network ACLs are stateless filters based on IP ranges, so following domains whose IP addresses change often would require building automation yourself, and there is also a rule quota. The condition to block direct IP connections eliminates the option that looks only at the DNS stage, and the condition that IP addresses change eliminates IP-based rules.

prompt: A new ticketing event service uses an Amazon DynamoDB table, and its traffic is unpredictable. Average utilization is normally below 5% of capacity, but within seconds after an event starts it spikes to dozens of times the average. The size of each event never exceeds twice the peak of the previous event, and throttling must not occur at those times. The table is currently provisioned for the peak, which is expensive. Traffic spikes happen once or twice a day, and the team cannot assign staff to capacity planning. The table is 20 GB, and both reads and writes increase during events. There is no hot partition problem in which requests concentrate on a single item. Which method is the MOST cost-effective without increasing the operational burden?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode so that it is billed only per request and handles the surging traffic without extra configuration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Keep provisioned mode, purchase 3-year reserved capacity to lower the unit price for the peak capacity, and set a capacity utilization alarm in Amazon CloudWatch.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Apply Application Auto Scaling to provisioned mode to adjust capacity automatically with a target utilization of 70%.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Place a DAX cluster in front of the table and reduce the table's provisioned capacity to the average usage level so that it absorbs the write load.

explanation: The correct answer is on-demand capacity mode. It is billed for requests made without capacity planning, so the idle cost of a table with low average utilization disappears, and it immediately accommodates up to twice the previous peak traffic, so surges of a similar size that repeat each time are handled without throttling (a surge exceeding double can be throttled within 30 minutes, so the precondition of this problem is important). Reserved capacity is effective for steady traffic, and with 5% utilization it would mean buying peak-sized capacity for a long term, which is very wasteful. Auto scaling takes time to react, so throttling can occur with traffic that spikes within seconds. DAX only caches reads and does not absorb write load, so reducing capacity would block writes. The two conditions of a spike that rises within seconds and no capacity-planning staff expose the weakness of approaches that set capacity in advance.

prompt: A platform team wants to let 300 developers create AWS Lambda execution roles themselves in the development account. However, developers must not be able to escalate their privileges by creating roles with greater permissions than their own, and the team wants to avoid an approach in which the security team approves every request. Developers must deploy new functions several times a day without prior approval, and the security team has 2 staff members. The security team wants to define the maximum permission scope of roles once. Developers create roles only within their own account, and the roles need only things like Amazon S3 read access and Amazon DynamoDB access. The security team already has one managed policy that defines the allowable permission scope. Which method is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Grant iam:CreateRole but add a condition that allows it only when the specified permissions boundary policy is attached together, to limit the maximum permissions of the role.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grant developers the IAMFullAccess managed policy, set an alarm on AWS CloudTrail events, and revoke excessive permissions after the fact when they are seen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Define an approval procedure in a document in which developers request role creation, and the security team receives the request as a ticket, reviews it, and creates the role on their behalf.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deny all of iam:* with an SCP in the development account, and create the necessary roles in a separate management account and share them across accounts.

explanation: The correct answer is a delegation approach that enforces a permissions boundary as a condition. If a condition on iam:PermissionsBoundary is attached to the iam:CreateRole allow, every role the developers create has only permissions within the boundary, so privilege escalation is prevented and no per-request approval from the security team is needed. IAMFullAccess lets developers create administrator permissions for themselves, and an alarm is only an after-the-fact response. A ticket approval process is the structure the requirements said to avoid. Denying all of iam:* with an SCP makes it impossible for developers to create roles at all, which contradicts the requirements. The requirement to define the maximum permissions once and let developers create freely within that scope is the classic use case for a permissions boundary.

prompt: A financial company must retain 120 TB of transaction records for 7 years under regulations. The data is retrieved only during audits, which happen once a year and are announced one week in advance, so it is enough if the data can be obtained within one day of a request. During the retention period, no one, including the root user, must be able to delete or overwrite objects. Once stored, the data is never modified, and about 2 TB of new data is added each month. The stored data consists of compressed files averaging 200 MB per object, and uploads are done in a monthly batch. Retention costs account for a large part of the annual IT budget, so management has asked for savings. Which storage approach is the MOST cost-effective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Upload to Amazon S3 with S3 Object Lock in compliance mode specifying a 7-year retention, and use a lifecycle rule to transition the objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Keep the data in S3 Standard-IA, have an administrator manually delete the objects after 7 years without using Object Lock, and review storage costs monthly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Keep the data in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval so that it can be retrieved immediately in milliseconds during audits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Store the data on Amazon EBS Cold HDD (sc1) volumes attached to EC2 instances and keep snapshots for 7 years.

explanation: The correct answer is the combination of Object Lock in compliance mode and a transition to Glacier Deep Archive. Compliance mode prevents anyone, including the root user, from deleting or overwriting objects during the retention period, and since retrieval once a year with restoration within a day is sufficient (standard retrieval takes within 12 hours), the cheapest archive class is the right fit. Standard-IA has a higher unit price per GB and, without Object Lock, cannot prevent deletion during retention. Glacier Instant Retrieval is for archives that need immediate access, so it is more expensive than required and has no deletion protection. EBS sc1 requires keeping volumes and EC2 instances running, and snapshots can also be deleted, so costs and management burden are much higher. The regulatory condition that deletion is impossible even for root and the retrieval condition that restoration within a day is acceptable decide the lock mode and storage class respectively.

prompt: A data analytics team queries CSV logs that accumulate in Amazon S3 at 300 GB per day by using Amazon Athena. Most queries use only a specific date range and a few columns, but a BI tool runs the same queries hundreds of times a day, and each time it scans all of the data, so it is slow and the scan-based charges are also large. The BI tool's SQL cannot be modified, and data transformation can be run as a once-a-day batch. The team does not want to add any new always-on infrastructure. Only 90 days of logs are queried, and there are 60 columns, but queries usually use only 5. The average scan per query is tens of GB, and BI dashboard responses take several minutes. Which method improves performance and cost the MOST effectively while keeping the query shape?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Compress the CSV files with gzip and change only the compression format in the Athena table definition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Load the data into an Amazon Redshift cluster and run subsequent queries in Redshift.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn on Transfer Acceleration for the S3 bucket to speed up Athena data reads.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Convert the data to Parquet with date partitions by using an AWS Glue job and update the table.

explanation: Athena charges in proportion to the amount of data scanned, so columnar Parquet reads only the needed columns, and date partitions make it read only the matching paths, greatly reducing scan volume and time while the SQL can be used unchanged. gzip compression reduces the scan volume to some extent, but it does not allow column-level reads or partition pruning. Loading into Redshift adds new infrastructure and a loading pipeline and does not fit the requirement of keeping the query shape. Transfer Acceleration is a feature for client upload and download paths and has nothing to do with Athena scans. The conditions that the SQL cannot be changed and that always-on infrastructure must not be added point to changing only the storage format and partitions.

prompt: An e-commerce company serves static assets through Amazon CloudFront, and the objects in the origin S3 bucket are encrypted with SSE-KMS using a customer managed key, and the bucket is not public. Users must not be able to access the S3 URL directly and must receive content only through CloudFront. User requests come from all over the world, and static files are downloaded millions of times a day. The key policy can be modified by the security team. There is one CloudFront distribution, which previously used an OAI, but object reads started to fail when SSE-KMS was introduced. The company wants to rework the origin access method. Which configuration meets these requirements MOST appropriately?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an OAI and allow only the OAI in the bucket policy; CloudFront will then decrypt and deliver SSE-KMS objects, so no key policy change is needed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Open the bucket to the public, have CloudFront add a secret Referer header, and use that header value as a condition in the bucket policy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create an Amazon S3 presigned URL for each object, set a short expiration behind CloudFront, and restrict direct access.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Associate an OAC with the distribution, allow only the cloudfront.amazonaws.com principal for that distribution in the bucket policy, and also allow decryption in the key policy.

explanation: The correct answer is the OAC configuration plus an allow in the key policy. OAC supports SSE-KMS objects, and allowing only a specific distribution in the bucket policy blocks direct access to the S3 URL. However, the KMS key policy must also allow the CloudFront service principal to decrypt. OAI does not support objects encrypted with SSE-KMS. The Referer header approach opens the bucket to the public and is bypassed if the header is exposed, so it is not secure. Presigned URLs must be issued and managed for as many objects as there are and are not a means of blocking direct access. CloudFront must read SSE-KMS objects, so an allow in the key policy is needed in addition to the bucket policy.

prompt: 300 web servers of an advertising platform generate thousands of JSON logs per second, and the logs are later queried with Amazon Athena. The company wants to convert them to Parquet format at roughly 1-minute intervals and store them in Amazon S3 by date. The small data team does not want to operate consumer application code or shard management itself, and the cost of keeping a cluster running at all times is also a burden. The schema of the logs is already defined in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Each log record averages 1 KB, and new fields are occasionally added. Records that fail conversion must be collected under a separate S3 prefix and checked later. Which method has the LEAST operational burden?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ingest into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and have a KCL consumer application on EC2 write Parquet files to Amazon S3.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run an always-on Spark Structured Streaming job on an Amazon EMR cluster and store the output in Amazon S3.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn on format conversion in an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream and specify a date prefix for the S3 destination.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Invoke an AWS Lambda function for each log record and store each one directly in Amazon S3 as an individual Parquet object.

explanation: Amazon Data Firehose is a serverless delivery service that handles buffering, JSON-to-Parquet conversion (using the schema of an AWS Glue table), and storing with an S3 date prefix through configuration alone, so there is no need to operate shards or consumer code. Data Streams with a KCL application requires shard management and operating EC2 consumers. An always-on EMR streaming job has large operational and cost burdens. Saving per record with Lambda causes an explosion of small files that degrades later analysis performance, and retries for failures and partitioning would also have to be implemented yourself. The condition of not operating shards, consumer code, or clusters points to a serverless delivery service.

prompt: A SaaS company receives events on an Amazon EventBridge custom event bus, and an AWS Lambda function that is a rule target processes them. An archive has been configured on this bus for the past month. Because of a bug in the deployed processing logic, about 6 million events were processed incorrectly over the last 3 days, and after the fix the same events must be processed again. The processing logic is idempotent, so the result is overwritten even if it receives the same event again, and the event publishers are owned by another team and cannot be modified. The archive retention period is indefinite, and all 6 million incorrectly processed events are included in the archive. Reprocessing must finish within one day, and no separate development staff has been assigned. Which method solves the problem with the LEAST effort?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Extract the events from Amazon CloudWatch Logs and call the publisher's API again with a script.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Specify that 3-day time range in the archive, replay it to the bus, and let the targets process the events again.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add an Amazon SQS dead-letter queue to the rule target and run reprocessing on the messages from the last 3 days.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase the asynchronous invocation retry count of the Lambda function so that past events are invoked again.

explanation: The original events are stored in the EventBridge archive, so replaying a specified time range lets the fixed target process the same events again without touching the publishers. Extracting events from logs and calling the publisher's API again is impossible without modifying the publishers and requires a lot of manual work. A dead-letter queue accumulates only events that failed delivery, so events that were delivered successfully but processed incorrectly are not in it. Asynchronous invocation retries only try failed invocations a few more times and do not recreate past events that already completed successfully. The fact that the processing logic is idempotent means there are no side effects even if the same events are delivered again.

prompt: A security team wants to turn on Amazon GuardDuty in all 60 existing accounts in AWS Organizations and in all accounts created in the future, and wants to view the findings in one existing security operations account. The organization keeps creating new accounts, and people logging in to each account to do the work must be avoided. The security team has three members and is not allowed to deploy agents on EC2 instances. The security account is separate from the log archive account, and the findings are connected to a notification system through Amazon EventBridge. Some accounts use only the Asia Pacific (Seoul) Region because of a Region restriction SCP. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Send an invitation to each member account and configure the connection by having the person in charge of each account accept it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Designate the security account as the GuardDuty delegated administrator.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Install a GuardDuty agent on the EC2 instances in each account and send the logs to the security account.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Set auto-enable for new accounts in the organization and also enable the existing member accounts in bulk.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Specify only the AWS CloudTrail logs of the management account as input and exclude other accounts from analysis.

explanation: The correct answers are designating a delegated administrator and configuring organization auto-enable. When the security account is the delegated administrator, the findings of all member accounts can be viewed in one place, and with auto-enable and bulk enablement, both existing and new accounts can be turned on without logging in. GuardDuty analyzes log sources directly without agents, so no installation on instances is needed. The invitation method requires acceptance in each account, which does not match the requirement to avoid manual work. Looking only at management account logs cannot detect threats in member accounts. Viewing in one place and enabling both existing and new accounts are separate requirements, so the actions are also split into two.

prompt: A security team sees several cases per month in which developers accidentally make an Amazon S3 bucket public, and it wants the public setting to be removed automatically as soon as a violation occurs. Three of the accounts need public buckets for static websites, so exceptions must be made. AWS Config is already turned on in all accounts. Maintenance of custom code must be minimized, and each account has dozens of buckets, so checking them one by one by hand has reached its limit. If possible, the time from detection to remediation should be within a few minutes, and automatic remediation records must be kept for audit purposes. The team judged that completely removing the permission to change S3 settings from developers is not realistic. Which method is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Receive AWS CloudTrail events with Amazon EventBridge and deploy to each account a self-written AWS Lambda function that checks and fixes bucket ACLs and policies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run an Amazon Macie discovery job every day to find public buckets and notify the owner so that they change the settings manually.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Check the bucket permissions check results of AWS Trusted Advisor once a week and block public access on violating buckets manually.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Detect public read access with an AWS Config managed rule, connect an AWS Systems Manager Automation document for automatic remediation, and exclude the exception accounts from the target.

explanation: The correct answer is the combination of an AWS Config managed rule and an automatic remediation action. The managed rule continuously evaluates the public read status, the attached Automation runbook reverts the setting without custom code, and the exception accounts can be excluded from the rule's scope. A self-built Lambda approach requires deploying and maintaining code in every account. Macie is a sensitive data discovery service and does not revert public settings. If a person checks Trusted Advisor once a week, the requirement for immediate remediation is not met. A managed configuration that satisfies all three conditions, automatic remediation, minimal code, and allowed exception accounts, is needed.

prompt: A company is moving two on-premises Windows file servers (with DFS replication) to AWS. 150 users at headquarters and branch offices use SMB shares and NTFS permissions based on Active Directory, and AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory is already integrated with the on-premises Active Directory. During an Availability Zone failure, the system must switch over automatically to another Availability Zone, and the company wants to leave server patching and replication management to AWS. Changes on the user side must be minimized, and the migration must be completed in one weekend day. The shared data is about 4 TB, and users mainly open and save office documents. Users must continue to connect with the same share names and paths. What should the company choose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Install the file server role on EC2 Windows instances in two Availability Zones and configure DFS replication yourself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a Multi-AZ Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system and join it to Active Directory.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a Multi-AZ Amazon EFS file system and mount it on the Windows instances over NFS.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Keep the data in an Amazon S3 bucket and provide it over SMB through an S3 File Gateway on EC2.

explanation: Multi-AZ FSx for Windows File Server natively supports SMB, Active Directory integration, and NTFS permissions, fails over automatically to a standby file server during an Availability Zone failure, and AWS manages patching and replication, so all constraints are met. Configuring DFS replication on EC2 yourself means continuing to operate patching and replication monitoring. EFS is NFS-based, so it is not supported on Windows instances and NTFS permissions cannot be used. S3 File Gateway is a cache over object storage, so file locking and permission behavior differ, and you would also be responsible for the availability of the gateway EC2 instance. The condition of keeping SMB and NTFS permissions as they are eliminates the NFS and object-based options.

prompt: An order service that processes about 500,000 orders per day directly calls three systems in sequence when an order completes: payment settlement, inventory update, and notification sending. If one of them is slow or down, the order fails. The three systems are operated by different teams and are sometimes down for hours at a time because of deployments. Events must not be lost even if one system is down for several hours, and each system must receive all of the same order events. Changes to the order service should be minimized to a single place in the publishing code. Each system takes a few seconds on average to process one event, and the processing order does not matter among them. Even the slowest system can catch up on several hours of events after recovery. Which configuration is MOST suitable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The order service publishes to an Amazon SNS topic, and the HTTP endpoints of the three systems subscribe directly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The order service publishes once to an Amazon SNS topic, and a dedicated Amazon SQS queue for each system subscribes to it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The order service publishes to a single Amazon SQS standard queue, and the three systems poll the same queue together.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add an exponential backoff retry loop to the order service that repeats calls to failed systems for up to 1 hour.

explanation: The publisher needs to send to Amazon SNS only once, and with a dedicated Amazon SQS queue for each subscriber, messages are retained in the queue even if one system is down for several hours and are processed after recovery, which provides both decoupling and loss prevention. With direct HTTP subscriptions, delivery is abandoned once the retry policy ends, so events can be lost during long outages. If three systems share one queue, each message is delivered to only one system and the other two never receive the event. A retry loop in the order service is still synchronous coupling, so order processing is delayed, and events are lost if the service restarts. The condition that all three systems must receive the same events and the condition of tolerating outages of several hours require fan-out and queue retention respectively.

prompt: A securities firm runs a 1.5 TB single-process in-memory analytics engine on Amazon EC2. The entire dataset must be loaded into memory, the engine is structured so that it cannot be split across multiple servers, and its average CPU utilization is low, at 20% or less. There is almost no disk I/O, and the instance is expected to be used continuously for more than a year. No schedule has been set for modifying the software. Memory usage is 1.3 TB at peak and is expected to grow by about 15% over the next year. The server is in a single Availability Zone in the Asia Pacific (Seoul) Region and is launched anew from an AMI in the event of a failure. Considering cost efficiency relative to performance, which instance family should the company choose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use several compute optimized instances, such as the C family, grouped together.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use storage optimized instances, such as the I family.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Distribute the engine across several general purpose instances, such as the M family.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use memory optimized instances, such as the X family.

explanation: When the entire dataset must be loaded into memory and CPU utilization is low, memory optimized instances such as the X family, which have a high ratio of memory per vCPU, are the most cost-effective. Compute optimized instances have a high vCPU ratio, so they waste CPU relative to memory. Storage optimized instances are for workloads where local disk I/O is important, and this analytics engine has almost no disk I/O. Splitting across several general purpose instances would distribute the single engine's dataset, which requires changing the application structure and also costs more. The condition that the engine cannot be split eliminates the options that distribute across multiple servers, and the low CPU utilization eliminates the vCPU-centric families.

prompt: A startup's B2B analytics dashboard uses Amazon Aurora MySQL. The database is about 300 GB with a read-heavy workload, and during business hours the load rises to 10 times its normal level, while it is nearly zero at night and on weekends. There is no DBA and two developers operate the system, so manually adjusting the instance size is difficult, and fixing a large instance sized for the peak is a cost burden. The company also wants to minimize connection drops during changes. Most queries are SELECT statements, and writes occur only in the nightly ETL. The average number of connections during business hours is around 200, and the application uses the cluster endpoint as it is. Which method has the LEAST operational burden?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use a provisioned db.r6g.4xlarge instance sized for the peak load, fixed 24 hours a day.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Switch to Aurora Serverless v2 and set an ACU range so that it scales out and in automatically.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Build your own scheduled AWS Lambda job that changes the instance class before and after business hours.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Always keep 15 Aurora read replicas and distribute all queries to the replicas.

explanation: Aurora Serverless v2 increases and decreases capacity almost continuously in ACU units according to the load, so it handles the peak without a DBA and reduces costs during idle times. Fixing a large instance means paying peak rates even at night and on weekends. Changing the instance class with a script causes brief interruptions and failover during the change, and you must maintain the scheduling logic yourself. Keeping 15 read replicas running at all times costs even more and does not reduce the write load. The conditions of minimizing interruptions during changes and having no DBA eliminate the manual class-change approach.

prompt: A design company stores about 40 TB of working files in S3 Standard. Restore requests usually arrive within a week after an incident. Incidents in which employees accidentally overwrite or delete files occur once or twice a month, and it must be possible to restore a previous version within 30 days. Storage costs must not grow without limit because of previous versions, and the company does not want to introduce a separate backup tool. There is only one IT person, so manual copy or cleanup procedures are hard to operate. The bucket has about 100 million objects with an average object size of 400 KB. Most restore requests are caused by overwrites, with about one deletion per month, and the versions to be restored are within the last 30 days. Which configuration is the MOST cost-effective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turn on bucket versioning only and keep all previous versions forever without lifecycle rules.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn on bucket versioning and add a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent objects after 30 days.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Switch the bucket to the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class to reduce the cost of objects that are not used often.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Copy the entire bucket to a second bucket every night with AWS DataSync to maintain daily copies.

explanation: Versioning keeps previous versions on overwrites and deletions, which makes recovery possible, and expiring noncurrent objects after 30 days meets the recovery-period requirement while limiting the cost of previous versions. Keeping all versions without a lifecycle rule makes costs grow continuously. Intelligent-Tiering is a means of saving costs based on access patterns, not a means of recovering from overwrites. Copying 40 TB every day with DataSync incurs large transfer and additional storage costs, and with only daily copies the point-in-time recovery resolution is also low. The condition that manual work cannot be operated also eliminates the daily copy approach.

prompt: A company plans to keep running six Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL db.r6g.2xlarge instances continuously for more than 3 years and has no plans to change the engine or Region. The company already purchased Compute Savings Plans last quarter, but its RDS bill did not decrease. RDS currently accounts for 35% of the total monthly AWS cost, and management wants commitment-based savings. The Multi-AZ configuration must be kept because of availability requirements, and DB operations must remain with AWS. The six instances have relatively constant CPU utilization 24 hours a day, and only minor version engine upgrades are planned. The finance team can choose the commitment type and the upfront payment ratio. Which method reduces RDS costs in the MOST cost-effective way?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Purchase RDS Reserved Instances for the relevant engine and Region and apply the commitment discount to instance usage hours.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase the hourly commitment amount of the Compute Savings Plans so that RDS instance hours are also included in the discounted usage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Move the RDS instances to EC2 r6g, install PostgreSQL yourself, and apply EC2 Instance Savings Plans.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change all instances from Multi-AZ to Single-AZ to eliminate the standby instance cost and shorten the backup retention period.

explanation: The correct answer is RDS Reserved Instances. Compute Savings Plans apply to EC2, AWS Fargate, and AWS Lambda usage and do not apply to RDS, so increasing the commitment amount does not reduce RDS costs. Reserved Instances fit long-term databases with a fixed engine and Region, and they also offer size flexibility within the same family. Installing on EC2 yourself means taking on patching, backups, and failover, which greatly increases the operational burden. Removing Multi-AZ reduces costs but lowers availability, which is a change in the opposite direction of the requirements. The conditions of keeping Multi-AZ and managed operations eliminate the options that downgrade the configuration or install it yourself.

prompt: A fintech company runs its service on an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster in us-east-1. Because of regulations, the company must keep a recovery environment in ap-northeast-2 to prepare for a failure of an entire Region, with an RPO of a few seconds and an RTO within a few minutes. The cluster is about 3 TB, and writes occur continuously. The team has three members and does not want to operate replication scripts or conversion jobs itself. The secondary cluster in Seoul is not used during normal operation and is promoted only during a failure. Overall write TPS averages 3,000, and DR drills are performed twice a year. Which method meets these requirements with the LEAST operational burden?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Copy automated snapshots to the Seoul Region every hour and, if a Regional failure occurs, create a new cluster and restore it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apply changes to a separate Aurora cluster in Seoul with an AWS DMS ongoing replication task.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add Seoul as a secondary Region to an Aurora global database and promote the secondary cluster during a failure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create an Aurora cluster in Seoul, configure binlog replication yourself, and promote it during a failure.

explanation: An Aurora global database replicates to another Region at the storage layer, usually with less than 1 second of lag, and fails over by promoting the secondary cluster, so it meets an RPO of a few seconds and an RTO within a few minutes with low operational burden. Copying hourly snapshots has an RPO of up to 1 hour, which does not fit, and restoring a new cluster also takes a long time. DMS ongoing replication requires task monitoring and schema management, which increases the operational burden, and its lag is not consistent. Binlog replication must be configured and monitored yourself, and its replication lag is larger than storage replication, so it is hard to guarantee the RPO target. The RPO of a few seconds eliminates the snapshot approach, and the condition of not operating it yourself eliminates the DMS or binlog approaches.

prompt: A company must interconnect 45 VPCs across 12 accounts and an on-premises data center connected over AWS Direct Connect. It has been building a mesh with VPC peering, but it has become hard to manage. The IP ranges do not overlap, transitive routing between VPCs is required, and changes when a new VPC is added must be minimized. The network team has three members and wants to manage routing policy centrally. Direct Connect is already connected through a Direct Connect gateway, and traffic between development and production environments must be isolated. Two or three new VPCs are added each month. Which configuration is MOST suitable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add VPC peering between every pair of VPCs to build a full mesh and manage the route tables.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a separate Site-to-Site VPN connection to on premises for each VPC and route through it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Configure a hub-and-spoke design in which the VPCs and Direct Connect are attached to an AWS Transit Gateway.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a PrivateLink endpoint service in each VPC and configure them to consume each other.

explanation: A Transit Gateway connects VPCs and on premises to a single hub and provides transitive routing, and a new VPC only needs to be attached to the hub, so changes are minimized. VPC peering does not support transitive routing, and a full mesh of 45 VPCs would need as many as 990 connections, which makes management even harder. Creating a VPN for each VPC makes connection count and bandwidth management complex, and transitive routing between VPCs would also have to be designed yourself. PrivateLink is a way of exposing specific services and does not suit connecting entire VPC networks. Central management, transitive routing, and easy VPC addition point to a hub structure.

prompt: An internal tool runs a CSV conversion job only three or four times a day, for 2 to 3 minutes each time. It currently keeps a t3.large EC2 instance running 24 hours a day and processes the job with cron, with CPU utilization below 1%. The results are stored in Amazon S3, and the input files are at most about 50 MB. The company also wants to reduce management tasks such as server patching, and the conversion logic is a single Python script. The job runs at fixed times during business hours, and a delay of a few minutes causes no problem. There are 40 such tools, so even though each individual cost is small, the total cannot be ignored. Which alternative is the MOST cost-effective while requiring only small code changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apply a 3-year Reserved Instance to the same instance to lower the hourly rate, leave the cron setup as it is, and add only a utilization alarm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduce the instance to t3.nano and keep cron running 24 hours a day, minimizing the hourly rate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Move the conversion logic to an AWS Lambda function invoked by Amazon EventBridge Scheduler, so that charges apply only for the time it runs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Move the conversion job to an AWS Fargate service, always run at least one task, and set the CPU to 0.25 vCPU.

explanation: The correct answer is the combination of EventBridge Scheduler and Lambda. The job takes about 10 minutes a day and each run fits within the 15-minute limit, so charges apply only for the execution time and number of requests, there is virtually no idle cost, and no server management is needed. A Reserved Instance leaves the waste of keeping a 1%-utilization instance running as it is and adds a commitment on top. A t3.nano is still a structure that runs 24 hours a day, so there is still idle cost, and it may run short of memory. An always-on Fargate task is also billed whenever it is running, so the same problem remains. Every always-on structure leaves idle cost, so a serverless approach that bills only for the time it runs is right.

prompt: A cost analysis SaaS vendor must read billing information in its customers' accounts. Customer security teams prohibit sharing long-term access keys and also want to prevent the confused deputy problem, in which the vendor mistakenly uses its role for another customer's request. The vendor has a service contract with them and must follow the principle of least privilege under the contract. There are 300 customers, so a separate authentication system cannot be built for each customer. The vendor fetches cost data once a day, and customers do not trust any external principal other than the vendor's account. The customer accounts are Organizations members and need only billing read permission. Which is the MOST secure method that meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a read-only IAM user and hand its access keys to the vendor, state in the contract that the keys must be rotated every 90 days, and review key usage with AWS CloudTrail.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a read-only IAM role in the customer account that trusts the vendor account, and add to the trust policy an external ID condition that the vendor assigns for each customer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a read-only role that trusts only the vendor account ID, and have all customers use the same role name and policy structure without an external ID.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Issue a temporary session of the customer's root user to the vendor so that it can connect to the billing console, and limit the session duration to 1 hour.

explanation: The correct answer is a cross-account role with an external ID condition. The vendor receives temporary credentials through AWS STS without long-term keys, and requiring a unique external ID per customer as a condition of the trust policy prevents the confused deputy problem, in which another customer tricks the vendor into using this role. Handing over an IAM user and access keys violates the policy of prohibiting long-term key sharing. A role without an external ID allows cross-account access but misses a step, so the confused deputy risk remains. Sharing a root session grants excessive permissions and is not an allowed approach. Prohibiting long-term keys and preventing the confused deputy problem require role delegation and an external ID respectively.

prompt: A regulatory auditor requires proof that the organization-wide API records to be retained for the next 3 years have not been modified or deleted during retention. An organization trail is already being delivered to an Amazon S3 bucket in the log archive account. The verification may be applied from the logs delivered going forward, tampering must be verifiable without additional development, and the auditor has read-only permission and must be able to reproduce the verification procedure personally. Write permission to the log archive account bucket is held by only two security administrators, and the log retention period is 3 years. The auditor plans to repeat the same verification every year. What should the company do to meet this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enable log file integrity validation on the trail and use the signed digest files to check whether the logs have been tampered with or deleted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Encrypt the trail logs with SSE-KMS and restrict the deletion permission in the key policy so that tampering cannot occur.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Also deliver the logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, specify a long retention period, and periodically compare the two copies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on versioning on the log bucket to preserve objects before modification and manually compare the version list during audits.

explanation: The correct answer is AWS CloudTrail log file integrity validation. When it is turned on, CloudTrail creates a hash for each delivered log file and delivers signed digest files to the same bucket every hour, and the auditor can reproduce with a CLI validation command that the logs have not been modified, deleted, or forged. It applies from logs delivered after it is enabled, so it must be turned on now. SSE-KMS is only encryption at rest and does not tell you whether tampering has occurred. Comparing CloudWatch Logs copies is manual, and the copy could be changed in the same way. Versioning preserves previous objects but is not a means of automatically proving tampering. The condition that applying it from the logs delivered going forward is acceptable means that turning the feature on now satisfies the requirement.

prompt: The delivery tracking system of a logistics company generates about 8 million events per day. Events of the same order (received, shipped, delivered) must be processed exactly once in the order in which they occurred, while events of different orders must be processed in parallel. The consumers are 20 Amazon EC2 workers, and the development team does not want to write code that manages queues per order. Each event averages 2 KB, and several hundred per second arrive at peak. Messages that repeatedly fail processing must be moved to a separate queue for a person to check. Which messaging configuration is MOST appropriate when building queue-based asynchronous processing that meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use an Amazon SQS standard queue, include a timestamp in each message, and have the consumers sort the messages before processing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Register each of the 20 workers as a subscriber to an Amazon SNS standard topic to fan out all events.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use an Amazon SQS FIFO queue with the order ID as the message group ID and use deduplication.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dynamically create an Amazon SQS standard queue for each order and have one worker poll each queue in sequence.

explanation: An SQS FIFO queue guarantees order within the same message group ID and ensures one-time processing with deduplication, and different groups can be consumed in parallel by multiple workers, so using the order ID as the group ID satisfies all the requirements. A standard queue does not guarantee order or deduplication, so consumer-side sorting cannot handle messages that arrive late. Fan-out with an SNS standard topic means all workers receive the same events, so they are processed in duplicate and with no order. Creating a queue per order causes an explosion of queues to manage and a single-worker bottleneck that harms parallelism. To satisfy both per-order ordering and parallelism across orders, order guarantees at the message group level are needed.

prompt: A B2B software vendor wants customers to use, privately from the AWS accounts of its 300 customers, an API that runs behind a Network Load Balancer in the vendor's VPC. The CIDR ranges of customer VPCs may overlap with each other and with the vendor's VPC, and the vendor does not want to expose the entire customer networks to each other. Traffic must not traverse the internet, and the vendor must not have to change its network configuration each time customers are added. Customers create an endpoint in their own account, and the vendor reviews and accepts the connection requests. The API exposes only HTTPS port 443, and the average call volume per customer is a few dozen requests per second. Which method meets these requirements with the LEAST operational burden?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Establish VPC peering between each customer VPC and the vendor VPC and add routes to each other's CIDR in the route tables.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a Transit Gateway, attach all customer VPCs, separate the route tables to divide the access scope, and approve an attachment each time a customer is added.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a VPC endpoint service with the NLB as the target, and have customers create an interface endpoint in their own VPC and approve each connection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the NLB to internet-facing and register a fixed IP address for each customer in a security group allow list to control access.

explanation: The correct answer is an endpoint service based on AWS PrivateLink. Consumers access only the one service through an interface endpoint, so overlapping CIDRs are not a problem and the entire network is not exposed, and the vendor does not need any routing changes even as the number of customers grows. VPC peering cannot be established when CIDRs overlap and results in connecting entire networks. A Transit Gateway also cannot route overlapping CIDRs. An internet-facing NLB with an IP allow list does not meet the private access requirement and increases the burden of managing customer IP addresses. The two conditions of overlapping CIDRs and service-level exposure eliminate all of the approaches that connect entire networks.

prompt: An e-commerce company is designing disaster recovery (DR) with an RPO of 5 minutes and an RTO of 1 hour. The database is an Amazon Aurora database of about 2 TB, and the application servers are configured automatically from AMIs and infrastructure as code (IaC) templates, so they can be launched anew in the DR Region at the time of a failure. Normally the DR Region does not receive user traffic, and its cost should be as low as possible. DR drills are held every six months. The database change rate averages a few MB per second and can be replicated continuously to the DR Region. The application server AMIs are copied to the DR Region regularly. Which DR strategy is the MOST cost-effective and meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Warm standby: run a scaled-down full stack in the DR Region at all times and scale it out with Auto Scaling during a failure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pilot light: continuously replicate only the database to the DR Region and launch the servers from AMIs and IaC during a failure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Backup and restore: copy nightly snapshots to the DR Region and restore the database from a snapshot during a failure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Active-active: both Regions process requests and traffic is distributed with latency-based routing.

explanation: Data can meet the 5-minute RPO through continuous replication, and since the servers may be launched at the time of failure, a pilot light that keeps only the core data tier running meets the requirements with the lowest normal-operation cost. Warm standby spends more on always-running servers for faster recovery than the requirement needs. Restoring from nightly snapshots has an RPO of almost a day and cannot meet the 5-minute target. Active-active operates both Regions in full, so it is the most expensive and also requires designing for write conflicts. The condition that servers may be launched anew at the time of failure makes a strategy of always-on servers unnecessary, and the 5-minute RPO requires continuous replication.
